title: Discovery and scoping
summary: How to turn a client's vague app idea into a small, signed, testable MVP before you quote or write a line of code.
youWillLearn: Why you never quote or build straight from a client's first description
How discovery finds the real problem behind a feature wish
How to write user stories with acceptance criteria a client can test
How to cut a wishlist down to an MVP and write the scope on one page

glossary.discovery: A short phase before the build where you learn the client's real problem, users and limits, and turn them into a plan.
glossary.MVP: Minimum viable product: the smallest version of the app that solves the core problem well enough to launch to real users.
glossary.user story: A one-line need written from a user's view: as a [who], I want [what], so that [why].
glossary.acceptance criteria: Concrete checks that prove a user story is done. If all pass, the story is finished; if not, it is not.
glossary.MoSCoW: A way to sort features into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time).
glossary.assumption: Something the plan takes as true without proof yet. Writing it down makes the risk visible to both sides.
glossary.scope creep: A project growing slowly through many small additions that nobody estimated or agreed to pay for.
glossary.change request: A written request for work outside the agreed scope, estimated and approved before anyone builds it.
glossary.spike: A short, throwaway experiment to learn how hard an unknown part is before you commit to a price.

steps.title: A wish is not a spec
body: Sam owns a small hair salon. On your first call she says: "I want an app where clients book, pay and get reminders. Maybe some AI too."
That sentence could be a two-week build or a six-month one. Quote it now and you are guessing. Start building now and you will probably build the wrong half.

callout.text: A client tells an architect: "a house with a nice kitchen". Nobody pours concrete yet. First come questions, then drawings, then a price.

scene.caption: Sam's idea arrives as one vague sentence. Its real size is unknown.

steps.title: Discovery turns a wish into an MVP
body: Before any estimate comes discovery: one or two sessions where you find the real problem behind the wish.
The output is an MVP: the smallest version that solves that problem for real users. Not a demo, and not every idea. The first thing worth launching.

callout.text: You already do this as a designer: research, problem framing, prioritizing. Discovery is the same craft, with a technical plan and a price at the end. Many freelancers charge for it as a small first project.

scene.caption: Discovery sits between the wish and the build. What comes out is small and clear.

steps.title: Ask about today, not about features
body: Ask what happens today. Sam answers the phone between haircuts. Clients call while she is cutting, and roughly one in ten forgets their appointment.
Now you have real problems: missed calls and no-shows. Keep asking: who books, how often, what does a no-show cost, and what would make this a success in three months?

callout.text: Write answers as numbers when you can. "About 1 in 10 no-shows" becomes your success metric later: did reminders bring it down?

scene.caption: Questions about today reveal two concrete problems behind the wish.

steps.title: User stories make features testable
body: Turn each need into a user story: as a [who], I want [what], so that [why]. Then add acceptance criteria: the checks that prove it is done.
Criteria end arguments. "Reminders work" is a feeling. "A text goes out 24 hours before each booking" is a test that you and Sam can both run.

code.code:
Story: As a client, I want to book online,
  so that I don't have to call during work hours.

Acceptance criteria:
- I see free slots for the next 4 weeks
- I pick a service, a stylist, then a slot
- A slot can never be booked twice
- I get an email confirmation within a minute
code.caption: Each criterion is something Sam can check herself on her phone.

scene.caption: Three needs become three stories. Each story gets checks that prove it is done.

steps.title: Must, should, could, won't
body: Sam's list will grow. Sort it with MoSCoW: must have for launch, should have soon, could have someday, won't have this time.
The MVP is the Must column only. Writing down the Won't column matters as much: it is the line you point to when someone says "I thought that was included".

callout.text: Packing a carry-on. Everything you want is on the bed. Only what fits goes in the bag, and you decide that at home, not at the gate.

scene.caption: Stories slide into columns. Only the Must column gets built first.

steps.title: Sketch the system behind the stories
body: Each Must story implies screens, data and outside services. Sketch them now, roughly. Booking needs a bookings table. Reminders need a scheduled job and an SMS or email provider.
This is where hidden size shows up. "Reminders" sounds like one feature, but it is three parts: a schedule, a message template and a provider account.

code.code:
create table bookings (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  client_id uuid not null references clients(id),
  stylist_id uuid not null references stylists(id),
  starts_at timestamptz not null,
  status text not null default 'confirmed',
  reminder_sent_at timestamptz
);
code.caption: A first sketch, not the final schema. It is enough to see the work and spot the unknowns.

scene.caption: The Must stories, drawn as parts. Payments are faded: not in the MVP.

steps.title: One page that Sam signs
body: Wrap discovery in one page: the problem, a success metric, the Must stories with criteria, the Won't list, and each assumption.
Assumptions are bets you say out loud: one location, English only, Sam supplies prices and photos. If one turns out false, the scope changes, and both of you saw it coming.

code.code:
Problem:  missed calls, ~1 in 10 no-shows
Success:  bookings online, fewer no-shows in 3 months

Must:     online booking, SMS reminders, owner calendar
Won't v1: loyalty points, native mobile app

Assumptions:
- One location, 4 stylists, English only
- Sam supplies services, prices and photos
- The salon pays SMS costs directly

callout.text: Claude Code can turn your call notes into stories and a scope doc in minutes. Then check: did it add features nobody asked for? Ask it to list assumptions and open questions separately. Does every Must story have criteria a non-developer can test?

scene.caption: Discovery ends with one signed page that both sides can point to.

steps.title: Scope creep and the vague AI feature
body: Scope creep rarely arrives as one big ask. It comes as ten small ones: "could it also…". Each sounds reasonable. Together they double the project.
AI features creep fastest, because "add some AI" has no finish line. Pin it down: what goes in, what comes out, and three real examples of a good answer. New ideas go through a change request.

callout.text: Never touch a risky integration for the first time after you quote. If the SMS provider or a calendar sync is unknown, run a short spike during discovery: a throwaway test to learn how hard it really is.

scene.caption: Small asks pile onto the signed scope. A change request gives each one a price first.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: A wish is not a spec. Discovery finds the real problem and shrinks it to an MVP: Must stories with acceptance criteria, a written Won't list and stated assumptions, on one page Sam signs.
Everything after that is a change request with its own estimate. Estimating is the next lesson.

quiz.question: On the first call Sam says: "Build me an app like the big booking platforms. How much?" What is the best next move?

options.text: Give a ballpark now so she does not lose interest.
options.why: A number said out loud sticks. With no scope behind it, it is either too low (you lose money) or too high (you lose the deal).

options.text: Propose a short discovery phase, then a written estimate.
options.why: Discovery turns "like the big platforms" into a small, specific MVP. Then the estimate has something real to rest on.

options.text: Start a prototype with Claude Code tonight to impress her.
options.why: Fast building of the wrong thing is still the wrong thing. You do not know yet which problem she most needs solved.

quiz.question: Which of these is a usable acceptance criterion for "clients get reminders"?

options.why: "Reliably" cannot be tested. You and Sam could each read it differently.

options.text: Reminders use a modern SMS API.
options.why: That describes how it is built, not what the client experiences. It does not prove the story is done.

options.text: Each client with a booking gets a text 24 hours before it.
options.why: It is concrete and checkable: make a booking, wait, see if the text arrives at the right time.

quiz.question: Halfway through the build, Sam asks: "Could the app also suggest the best time to rebook, with AI?" What do you do?

options.text: Write it up as a change request: inputs, outputs, examples, estimate.
options.why: It is outside the signed scope. A change request makes the new work visible and priced before anyone builds it.

options.text: Add it quietly; it is only one API call.
options.why: The API call is the easy part. Prompting, edge cases, testing and running costs add up, and you are now working unpaid.
The scope protects both sides; it is not a wall. Good ideas are welcome through the change process.

takeaways: Never quote or build from the first description. Run discovery first, ideally as a small paid step.
Ask about what happens today and capture numbers. They become your success metric.
Write user stories with acceptance criteria a non-developer can test.
The MVP is the Must column. Write the Won't list and your assumptions down too.
Anything new after sign-off is a change request: written, estimated, approved.
